Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPA View image in fullscreen Iranian missiles on display at the Azadi square in Tehran. Iran warned this weekend against any ‘adventurous action’ by the US. Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPA US-Israel war on Iran Trump climbs down on Iran strikes after Saudi alarm and threats from Tehran President claims delay is ‘subject to being able to rapidly make a deal’ as intervention by Saudi crown prince is revealed and Iran warns neighbours Guardian staff and agencies Sun 2 Aug 2026 00.45 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump said on Saturday night that the US would hold off on any new strikes on Iran provided a deal to end the months-long conflict is quickly reached – marking the president’s latest climbdown from extravagant threats to hit the Tehran regime hard. The Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump on Saturday to express concerns about his strike plans, it was reported. Trump’s reversal also came after Iran threatened to retaliate decisively against its neighbours in the event of US strikes, while Kuwait reported being hit by Iranian drones on Saturday and two ships were attacked off Oman in the strait of Hormuz. One source described as having knowledge of the Trump-Mohammed call told Axios that the Saudi crown prince had “urged Trump to de-escalate and refrain from launching the strikes”. The US war on Iran is spinning out of control | Mohamad Bazzi Read more The Associated Press also reported the conversation, citing its own source. It said the Saudis were concerned that if the US targets Iran’s energy infrastructure or carries out massive strikes on other key infrastructure, Tehran could respond by carrying out similar attacks on the kingdom and other Gulf countries. The crown prince during Saturday’s call sought clarity from Trump on what potential new action he was weighing to take against Iran, the Associated Press reported. A White House official, who was not authorised to comment publicly and requested anonymity, confirmed to the Associated Press that Trump and Prince Mohammed spoke on Saturday but did not offer any detail about the substance of their conversation. Saudi Arabia earlier this week joined the US in striking logistics and weapons sites used by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, but has been urging the US and Iran to get back to the negotiating table. CBS News reported that the US and Israel were planning joint strikes, possibly throughout the weekend, with oil refineries and power plants among possible targets. Iran warned this weekend against any “adventurous action” by the US and said it ⁠would retaliate decisively. Tehran foreign minister Abbas Araqchi’s comments in separate phone calls on Saturday with senior Turkish, Pakistani and Saudi officials came just hours after Kuwait’s army said it destroyed hostile ⁠drones launched by Iran against several vital facilities. A government facility in northern Kuwait and civilian property belonging to a company ​on Bubiyan Island were hit, with falling ​shrapnel causing material damage but no casualties, the Kuwaiti ​army said. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said on Saturday it had received reports of two maritime incidents off Oman, including one in which a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile that damaged the engine room. In the other incident, the master of a tanker reported seeing a large splash and an explosion close to the vessel, though no damage was reported. Iran’s Araqchi told regional counterparts that any attacks by the US and ​Israel or participation by regional countries in such actions would be ‌met with a “proportionate response”. Nournews, a ‌media outlet affiliated with Iran’s top security body, said on Saturday that US attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure would prompt Iranian strikes on oilfields in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, as well as the gasfields of Qatar and Israel. The developments appeared to have given Trump pause for thought, as he posted on Saturday night in characteristically grandiose language that “the USA is locked and loaded” to strike Iran with “military terror, strength, and power not seen since World War II”. Trump backtracks from promise to let Ukraine build Patriot missiles Read more “Despite this, we have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern countries, to hold off any attack,” he continued, adding that he would delay strikes “subject to being able to rapidly make a deal”. It would have to include “immediate, complete and total opening of the Hormuz strait, and an end to Iran’s nuclear threat”. Trump claimed that “the country of Israel joins me in this commitment”. However the government of Benjamin Netanyahu has previously disowned supposed agreements that were announced by the US president, such as the failed “memorandum of understanding” , and has been at odds with the Trump administration over how to proceed against Iran as well as its proxy Hezbollah operating from Lebanon. Log in here » Another person has pleaded guilty in a human smuggling case that involved the drowning of nine people in the St. Lawrence River as they tried crossing into the United States. Two families from Romania and India, along with the man allegedly piloting their vessel, died in March 2023 after they capsized while trying to enter the United States via Akwesasne Mohawk Territory. The U.S. Department of Justice said Thursday that Stephanie Square, 53, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit alien smuggling, four counts of alien smuggling for financial gain and four counts of alien smuggling resulting in death. Searchers look for victims Friday, March 31, 2023 after a boat capsized in Akwesasne, Que. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Ryan Remiorz Officials describe Square as a dual citizen from the Canadian side of Akwesasne. They also say she was the U.S.-based leader of a group that regularly smuggled people across the border via the Mohawk territory, which straddles Quebec, Ontario and New York state. “Aliens attempting to enter the United States illegally across the U.S.-Canada border are exposed to a range of dangers at the hands of human smugglers trying to capitalize on the misfortunes and misplaced hopes of others,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division in a statement. “Here, in the face of known dangers, the defendant directed her co-conspirators to smuggle a family with young children across the St. Lawrence River on a cold, windy night with limited visibility. The dangers materialized into a preventable and tragic loss of life.” Square’s charges only involved the deaths of the Romanian family, which included two children under the age of three. She is set to be sentenced on Nov. 25 and faces between five years and life in prison. Five other people previously pleaded guilty in the case. They are Dakota Montour, 32, and Kawisiiostha Celecia Sharrow, 45, from the U.S. side of Akwesasne; Janet Terrance, 46, of Hogansburg, N.Y.; and Timothy Oakes, 35, and Rahsontanohstha Delormier, 31, of Akwesasne on the Canadian side. The U.S. Justice Department said that during the week of March 27, 2023, a “prolific” Canadian smuggler contacted Square to smuggle the Romanian family across the St. Lawrence. Officials say she recruited multiple people to help, though one refused due to the high winds on the river that night. They say Square enlisted one of her regular drivers, Montour, to take the family to the residence of Timothy Oakes on Cornwall Island, described as a “notorious staging area for cross-border smuggling operations.” Officials say Oakes later took the family to a public boat launch on the island where his brother Casey picked them up and embarked on their ill-fated journey. The bodies of the migrants were pulled from the river in Akwesasne, about 130 kilometres southwest of Montreal, on March 30 and 31, 2023. The body of 30-year-old Casey was found in July 2023. The Romanian family was made up of Florin Iordache, 28; his wife, Cristina (Monalisa) Zenaida Iordache, 28; their two-year-old daughter, Evelin; and one-year-old son, Elyen. Both children were Canadian citizens and the family had been living in the Toronto area. The four other people who died were members of the Chaudhari family from the western Indian state of Gujarat. They included the father, Praveenbhai Chaudhari, 50; mother, Dakshaben, 45; son, Meet, 20; and daughter, Vidhi, 23. This report by The Canadian Press was first published July 23, 2026. https://www.dw.com/en/majority-of-german.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5LLo4 The German government has accused Russia of hybrid attacks Image: Florian Gaertner/photothek/picture alliance Advertisement In the past few weeks, Germany has seen a drone attack on Leipzig Airport and an arson attack near defense contractors in Bavaria, while explosive devices and pyrotechnics were found at two substations in Brandenburg and North Rhine-Westphalia . As the country enters a September featuring three vital state elections, attacks on critical infrastructure appear to be on the rise, and defense contractors are apparently in the crosshairs. After some initial hesitation, the German government has now publicly blamed Russia for the Leipzig attack, but could the Kremlin also be behind the other attacks? "We are not at war, but we are no longer at peace either," said Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt , of the Bavaria's conservatives, the Christian Social Union (CSU), has also warned that Germany has now become a "daily target of hybrid warfare," referring to measures that are not military, but are nonetheless meant to destabilize a country and unsettle the population — including cyberattacks, espionage, propaganda, disinformation, and acts of sabotage. The developments seem to have alarmed the German people. Some 56% of the eligible voters polled now see Germany's security as threatened by Russia, according to the latest Deutschlandtrend, for which the polling firm infratest-dimap conducted a representative survey of 1,319 German voters for public broadcaster ARD between August 31 and September 2. East Germans are significantly less concerned But not all Germans feel this way. Nearly half of citizens in eastern Germany , for instance, feel only slightly threatened, or not at all, by Russia. The same goes for supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), some of whose prominent figures have expressed support for Russia. The survey found that two-thirds of AfD supporters consider the threat from Russia to be low. The same divisions in the German population emerge on the question of arms exports to Ukraine. Just over half of Germans consider the country's military support for Ukraine appropriate, or think it should even be expanded, but for just over four in ten Germans, that support goes too far. Opposition to sending weapons to Ukraine predominates in eastern Germany and among AfD supporters. AfD holds steady lead nationwide The eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt will elect a new state parliament on Sunday, and the AfD continues to be way ahead in the polls and could even win an absolute majority — usually unheard of in German elections. The party also continues to enjoy strong support at the national level. The new poll suggests that if a general election were held this coming Sunday, the AfD would receive 27% of the vote, one point less than in August, which would make it the largest party in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag . The CDU/CSU, meanwhile, remains in second place at 21%, well below the 28.5% it managed in the Bundestag election in February 2025. The Greens would receive 15%, while the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the socialist Left Party have seen slight improvements compared to August, reaching 13% and 12%, respectively (+1 each). All other parties would fail to clear the 5% threshold. Unpopular government, unpopular chancellor The latest poll also suggests that the current governing coalition of the CDU/CSU and the Social Democrats would no longer have a majority if an election were held now. Only 15% of those surveyed are satisfied with the government's performance, and even among supporters of the governing parties themselves, a majority is disappointed with the incumbent coalition's performance. Chancellor and CDU leader Friedrich Merz fares even worse: Only 13% approve of his work. This is consistent with how citizens assess the CDU/CSU's competence. Also notable is that significantly fewer voters believe the CDU/CSU is capable of finding solutions in key policy areas. While just over a year ago, 31% still considered those parties competent to ensure peace in Europe, that figure has now dropped to just 23%. A similar loss of confidence in the CDU/CSU is apparent elsewhere: On asylum and refugee policy, on pension reform, and on climate and environmental policy. On the topic of the economy, the CDU/CSU still enjoys the highest level of public confidence at 24%, but here too, the figure has dropped significantly from 31% in February 2026. In eastern Germany, the AfD is now the party in which citizens place the most confidence across all policy areas surveyed, with the exception of climate and environmental policy. Is Germany's weak economy boosting the right-wing AfD? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Economy causing concern For many months now, Germans have viewed the economic situation as the most pressing problem to be solved. As many as 79% of respondents in the ARD Deutschlandtrend survey say the economy is doing poorly or very poorly. Here, too, however, there are significant differences depending on party affiliation. As many as 41% of SPD supporters view the economic situation as good or very good, and 37% of Green Party supporters say the same. In contrast, only 3% of AfD supporters share this view — they are much more pessimistic, with 96% saying the economy is poor or very poor. This article was translated from German. https://www.rte.ie/news/world/2026/0827/.text: Updated / Thursday, 27 Aug 2026 13:44 Getty Meta agreed to implement a series of changes to Facebook and Instagram The EU Commission is waiting on Meta to present changes to limit the addictive designs of its social networks, a commission spokesperson has said. Governments around the world are trying to curb children's access to harmful online content, including a world-first ban in Australia late last year on social media for children under 16. "We have been very clear .. we expect proper screen time management, we expect proper parental control on these platforms. Meta knows ... the ball is in Meta's court," the commission spokesperson said. In a statement, the Irish Department of Communications said there were investigations ongoing into whether some social media platforms are in breach of obligations to protect children online. It said the European Commission was preparing proposals for additional legislation to further enhance protection of children online and are expected in the next few months. "As the protection of children and young people online is a key theme of Ireland's EU Presidency, we will give priority to the negotiations on those proposals as soon as they emerge," it said. The Government has previously expressed support for social media restrictions for children but has repeatedly said its preference would be for any ban to be implemented at EU level. Last month, the EU charged Meta's Instagram and Facebook with breaching its technology rules , with regulators targeting features they say are designed to keep users hooked and demanding changes to autoplay and infinite scroll or risk fines. The European Commission said Meta had failed to adequately assess the addictive risks posed by highly personalised recommendations, autoplay and infinite scroll. Meta said in a statement at the time that it disagreed with the findings, saying they did not take into account the "significant steps" the company had taken to protect teenagers. Call for new Meta measures to be applied globally Earlier, South Korea's media regulator said measures proposed by Meta to curb potentially addictive features for young users should ideally be applied worldwide, The Korea Media and Communications Commission (KMCC) said in a statement that social media companies needed to take greater responsibility for protecting children and teenagers and pointed to seven bills pending in the country's parliament aimed at strengthening youth protections online. The commission "believes that in order to create an environment in which Korean youth can use social networking services safely, it is necessary to strengthen social media providers' responsibility to protect minors," the regulator said. The comments followed landmark US settlements announced yesterday under which Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion and implement a series of changes to Facebook and Instagram after several states accused the company of designing products that contributed to youth addiction and harmed mental health. The measures include limits on usage time, restrictions on notifications, stronger age-verification tools, the option of non-algorithmic feeds and hiding "likes" and similar engagement metrics for younger users. The KMCC said that, among Meta's proposed corrective measures, changes to features that may encourage excessive use, including algorithm-based content recommendations, display of engagement metrics such as likes, and push notifications designed to draw users back onto platforms, "would ideally be applied to youth users worldwide as well". South Korea has also been moving toward stricter oversight of social media use by minors amid growing concerns about excessive screen time and the role of recommendation algorithms in keeping young users engaged. The debate mirrors a broader global push to protect children online, though proposed restrictions on minors' social media use have drawn criticism over privacy concerns and questions about enforcement. British government expects Meta's new protections to apply in UK In the UK, the British government expects Meta's new protections for teenagers to also apply in Britain. British Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said he did not want young people in America to have "a higher rate of protection" than young people in Britain. However, he added that the UK Government is also going further and will implement a social media ban for young people next year. This morning, Poland's minister of digital affairs said he has asked the European Commission to impose a €250m fine on Meta. "I also call on Meta to immediately introduce effective tools to eliminate scams, false advertising, and the promotion of illegal applications," Krzysztof Gawkowski posted on X. Meta deal shows firms can protect young users, Australia says Australian regulators meanwhile said Meta's move to restrict teenagers use of social media shows companies have tools to better protect young people online. Australian Communications Minister Anika Wells said social media companies "have the tools at their disposal to protect young people from their addictive features but have chosen not to use them". "That's why Australia took world-leading action to create a minimum age for social media, and we are proud that more than 20 countries are joining us," she added. In the US, social media companies still face thousands of lawsuits in federal and state courts by individuals, school districts, municipalities and other government entities claiming they knowingly sought to addict children and caused a mental health crisis including harms such as anxiety, depression and suicide. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: NSW domestic violence rental reforms in effect from today Rental reforms which make it easier for victim-survivors of domestic violence to leave a rental property in NSW are in effect from today, the state government says. Under the changes, victim-survivors no longer need to notify people they share a lease with they are leaving a rental property, cannot be held responsible for damage caused by domestic and family violence, and must be asked for permission to publish images of the property that show their belongings. The government says victim-survivors have now have broader rights to change locks without landlord consent. The NSW fair trading minister, Anoulack Chanthivong, said the reforms “deliver on the Minns Labor government’s promise to make renting fairer by replacing unsafe, outdated laws with practical, compassionate protections which put victim-survivors first”.
